source.title: On Weak-to-Strong Generalization and f-Divergence
source.authors: Wei Yao; Geng-Ze Xu; Huayi Tang; Wen-Kai Yang; Dong-Lin Di; Zi-Qiao Wang; Yong Liu

record.file_problem: The paper text is present through the appendices. Some figure text and plotted values are garbled in the extraction; Table 2 values are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper analyzes weak-to-strong training theoretically and compares alternative f-divergence training losses with cross-entropy, but it does not calculate PGR or report weak-supervisor and strong-ceiling scores.
record.gate_note: The experiments vary the loss, noise level, dataset, and GPT-2 supervisor/student pair, and report test accuracy. Those accuracy comparisons do not establish PGR because the paper does not report the weak supervisor’s or strong ceiling’s performance. Theoretical statements about convergence to the weak model do bear on the basic effect and the theory version. Figure 1 and Figure 2 are only included as qualitative aggregate rows where the text explicitly describes their results.
record.test_reason: The paper compares alternative f-divergence training losses against cross-entropy for weak-to-strong (W2S) fine-tuning of GPT-2 students on weak labels. For a fixed supervisor and ceiling, PGR rises with student accuracy, so these comparisons bear directionally on V2. Its theory (Thm 4.1, Cor 4.1, Thm 4.2) bounds student performance near the supervisor's, which bears on V1 and V5. No weak-supervisor or ceiling accuracy is reported, so PGR itself is never computed.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors also claim that Jeffreys and reverse KL consistently beat CE, that Hellinger is the most robust loss under moderate noise, and that χ2 and JS beat CE at 50% noise. Theoretically, the student is bounded by supervisor quality and misfit, and different f-divergence losses are equivalent under confidence regularization.
record.recipe_differences: Uses weak-model labels to fine-tune stronger pretrained GPT-2 models, but studies f-divergence loss variants in reward-modeling classification, including controlled label noise, rather than measuring PGR in the original setup.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported test accuracy varies with loss, dataset, weak-label noise level, supervisor/student pair, and confidence-enhancing regularization.

fits_no_version.finding: Theorem 4.3: any f-divergence loss plus confidence-enhancing regularization is equivalent to another f-divergence loss with a transformed regularizer.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Loss choice under auxiliary confidence loss is theoretically interchangeable given suitable regularizer transforms.

record.problems: PGR is not calculated and neither weak-supervisor nor strong-ceiling test performance is reported. The paper reports no uncertainty estimates for the empirical comparisons. Figure values are not recoverable in the supplied extraction. The text's claim that Pearson χ2 and JS consistently improve by at least 1% at 50% noise has exceptions in Table 2.
record.rows_left_out: To stay within 60 rows, omitted the Table 2 numeric entries for reverse KL, Jeffreys, and KL across both datasets and all six supervisor/student pairs. Table 2 reports these values separately; the text also describes some aggregate findings for these losses. The retained rows prioritize CE and Pearson χ2, Hellinger, and JS comparisons.

untested.parts: No empirical weak-supervisor accuracy, ceiling or PGR is reported, so whether students beat supervisors is unmeasured.
Ensembling weak supervisors is not tested. Loss effects are given as student accuracy only, not as PGR.
PGR is not reported across sizes or tasks, and no predictors are analysed.
Distribution shift, exploitation of the supervisor, and error correlation are not tested.
No vision or other non-language modality is used.

missing.what: Numeric test accuracies for each loss at noise 0.0–0.4 and with confidence regularization; the extraction is garbled.

record.verdict_notes: Noise is artificially injected into the weak labels, and at 50% noise accuracies sit near or below chance, so treat those V2 links cautiously. Rows left out (declared in rows_left_out) show reverse KL far below CE on CAI-Harmless at 50% noise (e.g. 30.18 vs 40.38), which undercuts the authors' 'consistently outperform' claim for reverse KL. No uncertainty is reported for any empirical comparison.

versions.untested_parts: No empirical PGR, weak-supervisor test accuracy, or strong-model ceiling is reported; the relevant evidence is theoretical and conditional.
The loss variants are compared by test accuracy, but the paper does not report PGR or establish that they raise PGR over naive fine-tuning.
Although model pairs and two reward-modeling datasets are varied, PGR is not reported and representations are not analyzed as predictors.
No experiment tests distribution shift or whether gains shrink when weak and strong models err alike.
The analysis gives limits and an asymptotic overfitting case, not a general characterization of all conditions that guarantee a student beats its supervisor.
Experiments are classification/reward modeling; vision and other modalities are not tested.

relationships.condition: Theoretical: infinite data with perfect overfitting to weak labels
relationships.reason: The theory says the student converges to the weak model's performance, so a positive gap needs controlled optimization such as early stopping (TH3). TH1 and TH2 bound the gap two-sidedly without showing a gain.
relationships.display_finding: The student converged to weak-model performance, so positive gains required controlled optimization such as early stopping.
